title: Normal labour: stages and progress
summary: Recognising the stages of labour and what counts as normal progress in a low-risk pregnancy.

blocks.heading: Latent first stage
bullets: Painful contractions with some cervical change, including effacement and dilatation up to around 4cm.
Can last many hours, especially in a first baby — support at home with analgesia and reassurance unless there are concerns.
Not itself a reason for admission unless there are other concerns (reduced movements, bleeding, ruptured membranes, maternal request for assessment).

blocks.heading: Established (active) first stage
bullets: Regular, painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation from around 4cm to full dilatation.
Offer the full range of pain relief options and discuss preferences for the rest of labour.
VERIFY local observation frequency (maternal pulse/BP/temperature, contraction frequency, fetal heart) — this is set by local protocol and NICE intrapartum care guidance.

blocks.heading: Second stage
bullets: From full dilatation to birth of the baby — has a passive phase (before the urge to push) and an active (pushing) phase.

VERIFY local definitions of 'delay' in second stage — commonly discussed as around 2 hours without an epidural / 3 hours with one in a first baby, and around 1 hour without / 2 hours with one in a subsequent baby, but exact local thresholds and escalation steps should be confirmed against current protocol.
Delay in progress should prompt reassessment of contractions, position, and fetal wellbeing, and discussion with the obstetric team per local pathway.

blocks.heading: Third stage
bullets: From birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes.

Active management (uterotonic drug plus controlled cord traction) is generally recommended over physiological management, as it's associated with a lower risk of postpartum haemorrhage — discuss the choice with the woman antenatally where possible.
VERIFY local uterotonic drug/dose/timing protocol before administering.
A third stage lasting longer than expected, or any heavy bleeding, should prompt escalation — see the Major obstetric haemorrhage emergency drill.

blocks.heading: If something isn't right
bullets: This is a general orientation to normal progress, not a substitute for continuous clinical assessment.
See the Major obstetric haemorrhage, Cord prolapse, and Shoulder dystocia emergency drills for red-flag intrapartum events.
